questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a trust boundary sits
questions.learningObjective: Describe where a trust boundary sits in a field deployment.
questions.stem: Explain where a trust boundary sits in a distributed survey deployment and why its position matters.

answer.exemplar: A trust boundary is the line across which data changes trust level, so it is drawn where information crosses from something the team controls into something it does not. In a survey deployment the boundary usually runs around the shared service: the handheld, the relay and the local store are inside it, while the public network, the cloud provider and any third-party map tile service sit outside it. The position matters because everything crossing the line is subject to checks, and everything on the wrong side of the line is treated as untrusted regardless of how carefully it was set up.

questions.explanation: The boundary marks where control and trust change, so it decides what needs checking and what must be assumed hostile. Drawing it around convenience rather than ownership weakens every control on it.
questions.hint: Draw the line where control passes out of the team's hands.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Explaining a rise in exposed listeners
questions.learningObjective: Explain how exposed listeners can rise without new devices.
questions.stem: Explain how an increase in exposed listeners can happen without any new device being deployed.

answer.exemplar: The count can rise on the same hardware because listening is a configuration state rather than a property of the box. A relay that starts a diagnostic service after a firmware update, a handheld that begins syncing over a public link, a firewall that opens a port for a partner integration, or a monitoring agent that starts answering health checks all add listeners without adding devices. That is why the count must be read alongside the reason each listener exists: the team may remove the listener rather than the kit, and a rising count is a prompt to ask what changed rather than evidence of new equipment.

questions.explanation: Listeners follow configuration changes, so the same kit can expose more over time. Removing the listener rather than the device is often cheaper, which a rising count alone would not show.
questions.hint: Think about configuration, not boxes.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Reading an inventory for exposure
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to read an inventory so the exposure picture is trustworthy.
questions.stem: Explain how to read an equipment inventory so that the exposure picture is trustworthy.

answer.exemplar: Read the inventory for reachability, data held and consequence, not for completeness of paperwork. For each line ask whether the device answers requests from outside the survey network, what data it holds while it does so, and what an attacker would gain by reaching it. Record the reach column explicitly, because a device that is offline by default and one that is merely switched off differ in risk even when both are present on the list. Where reach is unknown, mark it unknown rather than assuming it is low: an unverified line is a measurement gap, and treating it as safe is how blind spots survive into the field.

questions.explanation: The inventory is only useful when reach, data and consequence are recorded per line, with unknowns marked as unknown. Assuming a gap is safe is what lets an unassessed device travel into the field.
questions.hint: Read each line for reach, data and consequence.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Why a threat list is applied element by element
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a threat list is worked one element at a time.
questions.stem: Explain two reasons a threat list must be applied one element at a time.

answer.exemplar: First, each entry describes a different combination of asset, actor, weakness and consequence, so a blanket control will either be too broad for one entry or too narrow for another. The right answer to a shared storage misconfiguration is not the right answer to a lost handheld, and treating the list as one item produces controls that fit neither. Second, working elements separately is what makes the response measurable: each entry can be closed, retested and reported on its own, so the team can see which treatment actually worked. A list handled as a whole gives a single story that hides both the mismatched controls and the untested ones.

questions.explanation: Elements differ in substance, so a blanket control fits none well, and separate treatment makes closure and retesting possible. Handling the list as one item hides mismatched and untested controls.
questions.hint: Ask what each entry needs and how it gets closed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A stage of the threat model left out
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a threat model stage adds over a threat checklist.
questions.stem: Explain what a threat model stage adds that a checklist of threats does not.

answer.exemplar: A checklist of threats is a list of things that could go wrong, and it says nothing about which are true for the system in front of you. A threat model stage adds the context that makes the list actionable: it establishes what the system actually is, where the boundary runs, what each asset holds and who could reach it, and it forces the team to rank the findings so effort goes where consequence is highest. Without that stage the list is a set of generic possibilities, and a control chosen from it can easily address an entry that does not apply here while missing the one that does.

questions.explanation: A model stage adds system context, reach and ranking to a generic list of possibilities. Without it, controls can be aimed at entries that do not apply while the real exposure is left untouched.
questions.hint: Ask what the list cannot tell you on its own.

questions.topic: Data selecting an action
questions.learningObjective: Explain how survey data can select an action.
questions.stem: Explain how data in a survey table can select an action rather than merely describe one.

answer.exemplar: A table selects an action when each row carries a value that can be compared against a stated threshold, and the comparison ends in a decision rather than an observation. A reach score of 8 beside a threshold of 6 does not merely report that a device is reachable; it assigns that device to a control list, assigns the work, and makes the row visible until it is closed. For this to work the threshold has to be written down before the data is collected and applied unchanged, otherwise the table drifts into a description that nobody can be held to. The value of the table is that the rule is public, so a reader can check the arithmetic and disagree with the threshold itself.

questions.explanation: Data selects an action when a stated, pre-committed threshold turns each row into a decision. Without a written rule the table only describes, and nobody can check the working.
questions.hint: Ask what makes a row become someone else's work.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Where a trust boundary sits
questions.learningObjective: Explain trust boundary placement and the effect of placing it wrongly.
questions.stem: Explain how a misplaced trust boundary misleads a survey team and where the line belongs.

answer.exemplar: A trust boundary is drawn where the survey's control over its data ends, which is normally at a shared external service such as a cloud account, a partner integration or a mapping provider. Its position matters because it decides what is checked, what is trusted and where controls are placed. Draw it too far out and the team treats a service it cannot administer as its own, skipping the checks that a third party might not apply. Draw it too far in and the team checks its own kit repeatedly while the real crossing point, where data actually leaves, is left unexamined. Both mistakes produce the same symptom: a survey that believes it is protected.

questions.explanation: The boundary decides what is checked and where controls sit, so a misplaced line produces false confidence in either direction. A team that believes it is protected is the result of both errors.
questions.hint: Ask where the team's control actually ends.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Reading an inventory for exposure
questions.learningObjective: Describe how to present an inventory so readers can judge exposure.
questions.stem: Explain how to present an inventory so that readers can judge exposure for themselves.

answer.exemplar: Present the inventory per item and per item only, because a summary hides the cases that matter. For each line give the asset, whether it is reachable from outside, what it holds, and the consequence if it were reached, with unknowns written as unknown rather than left blank. Then state the date the reach was checked and who checked it, so a reader can judge how stale the answer is. Readers can then apply their own threshold to the same evidence and reach their own conclusion, which is what makes the document usable by people with different appetites for risk rather than a single number that has to be trusted.

questions.explanation: Per-item detail with reach, data, consequence and a check date lets a reader apply their own threshold. A summary figure or a blank cell hides the cases that matter and forces trust.
questions.hint: Give per-item facts a reader can re-read.

questions.topic: Where a trust boundary sits
questions.learningObjective: Compute the score for a worked example in a brief.

stimulus.body: A worked example in the survey guide shows a shared relay with a likelihood of 4 and an impact of 7, and notes that a proposed change would halve the likelihood without touching the impact.

questions.stem: Using the worked example, what value does the calculation produce for that entry?

options.text: The score is 11, because 4 plus 7 is the total once the two inputs are combined.
options.misconception: adds the two inputs instead of multiplying them

options.text: The score is 56, because both inputs are doubled before the multiplication is carried out.
options.misconception: doubles both inputs before multiplying them

options.text: The score is 14, because the halved likelihood is used while the impact is ignored.
options.misconception: applies the proposed change before scoring and drops impact

options.text: The score is 28, because 4 times 7 gives that figure for the entry as it stands.

questions.explanation: Four times seven is 28 for the entry as recorded, and the proposed change is assessed separately. Adding the inputs, halving one or doubling both produce a figure that cannot be compared.
questions.hint: Multiply the two values as they are recorded.

questions.topic: Data selecting an action
questions.learningObjective: Decide which rows clear the threshold and count them.
questions.stem: Decide which rows clear the threshold, then compute the number of rows that do.

options.text: No rows clear it, since a threshold of 6 cannot be applied to a table of mixed values.
options.misconception: claims a threshold cannot apply to mixed data

options.text: Six rows clear it, because a row at 6 also counts as reaching a threshold of 6.
options.misconception: treats a row at the threshold as below it

options.text: Three rows clear it, since only the rows scoring 12, 9 and 7 reach the threshold of 6.
All rows clear it, because every row in the table was scored against that same threshold.
options.misconception: counts rows that scored below the threshold

questions.explanation: The threshold is six, so the rows at 7, 9 and 12 clear it, which is three rows. Including the row at six, excluding everything or counting all rows each applies another rule.
questions.hint: Apply the stated threshold and count what passes it.
